title: Decisions and loops
body: `if (condition) { ... } else if (...) { ... } else { ... }` runs the first branch whose condition is true. The condition must be a `bool`; C# does not treat 0 or null as false, so `if (count)` is a compile error. Always use braces for multi-line branches.

A `switch` statement selects a section by matching a value against `case` labels; each section ends with `break`, `return`, `throw` or `goto case` because C# forbids silent fall-through between non-empty sections. Several labels may share one section. Later stages replace many switch statements with switch expressions and patterns.

`while (condition)` checks before each iteration and may run zero times. `do { ... } while (condition);` checks after, so the body runs at least once. `for (init; condition; step)` packages a counter loop. `foreach (var item in collection)` visits each element of anything enumerable without manual indexing.

`break` leaves the innermost loop or switch; `continue` skips to the next iteration of the innermost loop. To leave nested loops in C# 14, extract a method and `return`, or use a flag. C# 15 adds labeled break/continue, covered in the final stage.

A `foreach` loop variable is read-only, and the collection must not be modified while it is being enumerated (a List throws InvalidOperationException). Before writing a loop, check the termination condition, whether the body may run zero times and whether anything mutates the collection being walked.

question: Which loop always executes its body at least once?
reasoning: do ... while tests its condition after the body, so the first iteration always runs.
